title: Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (2014 Budget Measures No. 1) Bill 2014
short_title: Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (2014 Budget Measures No. 1) Bill 2014

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill enacts a range of savings and benefit changes from the 2014 Budget, mostly affecting welfare recipients and family payments.
It alters payment rules, including freezing some income thresholds, changing how certain payments are indexed, and adjusting eligibility and portability conditions.
It also adds a recent Western Australian pay equity decision to the special account, enabling Commonwealth support for affected service providers.
changes: It stops the seniors supplement for holders of two specified health cards in June 2014.
It renames the clean energy supplement and stops its annual increases permanently from July 2014.
It pauses for three years the indexation of income and asset limits for most working-age allowances and family tax benefit free areas.
It changes parenting payment single indexation to the consumer price index and removes the link to male average earnings.
It limits overseas portability for student payments to six weeks and extends the ordinary waiting period for working-age payments.
It freezes certain family tax benefit rates for two years and adds the specified pay equity decision to the special account.
summary.affected: Recipients of working-age allowances, student payments, family tax benefits, parenting payment single, seniors supplement, and service providers affected by the Western Australian pay equity decision.

speeches.speaker: Kevin Andrews
speeches.brief: Introduced the second Social Services budget bill, confirming the pension age would rise to 70 by 2035, the family tax benefit B primary earner threshold would fall from $150,000 to $100,000, and a $3 million Young Carer Bursary Program would fund about 150 bursaries annually for young carers.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Moved the day's final debate management motion, capping debate on two Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment budget bills at 3 hours for the second reading and 30 minutes for consideration in detail, to pass them to the Senate by week's end.

speeches.speaker: Jenny Macklin
speeches.brief: Opposed the Social Services budget bills, citing Australian Council of Social Service modelling that pensioners will be $80 a week worse off within a decade, and NATSEM analysis showing about 1.2 million families will be on average $3,000 a year worse off by 2017-18, while the government proceeds with a $22 billion Paid Parental Leave scheme.

speeches.speaker: Brendan O'Connor
speeches.brief: Opposed the Social Services budget bills, noting Australia's welfare spending is just 8.6 per cent of GDP compared with an OECD average of 13 per cent, and calculated that job seekers aged 22 to 24 moved from Newstart to Youth Allowance would lose about $48 a week, an 18 per cent income cut.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Defended the Social Services budget bills, projecting they would reduce debt from a forecast $667 billion to $389 billion within a decade, warned Australia's worker-to-pensioner support ratio will fall to about 2.7 to one by mid-century, and noted a review of a rule that let disability pensioners travel overseas for 19 weeks while still receiving payments.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: Opposed the Social Services bills, calculating that changing pension indexation would leave a single pensioner in his Charlton electorate about $1,500 a year worse off over four years, and contrasted the $50,000 Paid Parental Leave payment available in wealthier electorates with the under $20,000 that more than 80 per cent of Charlton women would receive.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: Defended the Social Services bills, citing life expectancy in some of his western electorate's towns being 15 years lower than in wealthy urban areas, and highlighted a $1.6 million Get Real Program under which young people, mostly Aboriginal, pledge to be in education, training or work by their 17th birthday.

speeches.speaker: Rob Mitchell
speeches.brief: Opposed the Social Services bills, noting 29,995 families in his McEwen electorate receive family tax benefits that would be cut, quoted a self-described Liberal-voting Puckapunyal chaplain's constituent email warning of harm to volunteer-reliant single-income families, and cited National Seniors Australia's Michael O'Neill on retirees' inability to absorb sudden bill spikes.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Defended the Social Services bills, breaking down the $415 billion 2014-15 budget to show $146 billion goes to social security, including $42 billion for income support for seniors alone, and cited an estimate that each month of delay in passing these measures would cost taxpayers more than $117 million.

speeches.speaker: Jenny Macklin
speeches.brief: Moved a package of opposition amendments to both Social Services budget bills, seeking to strip out measures including changes to pension indexation, the pension age increase and family tax benefit freezes, but declined to elaborate given the government's gag motion limiting debate time.
